pr_title: Support HTTP persistent connections in Web Cmdlets
pr_body:
<!-- Anything that looks like this is a comment and can't be seen after the Pull Request is created. -->

# PR Summary

Fis #12764

This PR addresses [12764](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/issues/12764) by using persistent HTTP connections when Invoke-WebRequest uses the -Session variable. It does this by 
1. Tracking the  HttpClient object in the saved WebRequestSession.
2. Monitoring properties in WebRequestSession and rebuilding the HttpClient if they are changed. This is done to ensure that existing scripts that might tweak parameters between invocations of IWR actually apply the changes so they will behave in a backwards compatible manner. When anything that impacts the HttpClient is changed, the persistent connection is abandoned by disposing the HttpClient and underlying HttpClientHandler and constructing a new one. A warning is logged when this occurs as it has a performance impact (though no worse than the existing behaviour).
3. To support point 2, many parameters are stored as internal set-only properties in the WebRequestSession so changes between invocations that would require a new connection can be detected and the handler rebuilt appropriately.

## PR Context

This PR makes a considerable difference to performance when using Invoke-WebRequest or Invoke-RestMethod with sessions when multiple requests are made to the same host. This is particularly evident for HTTPS requests, as each HTTPS connection can take hundreds of milliseconds to establish.

This PR as written passes existing tests in `WebCmdlets.Tests.ps1` and additional WebSession tests that verify the HttpClient is rebuilt when appropriate.

The PR provides as much backwards compatibility as possible at the expense of the complexity of tracking how the HttpClient used in the WebSession was constructed and recreating the HttpClient in the case it would have been constructed differently between invocations in scripts that assume it is okay to change parameters between invocations with the same WebSession.

This PR squashes the commits in the original PR#19173 following multiple round of reviews by @iSazonov and @CarloToso on a previous version of the PR. PR#19173 has been withdrawn due to number of commits and volume of review comments.

## Performance Impact
Performance impact of maintaining HTTP connection persistence is measured by comparing PowerShell 7.3.3 with this PR using this simple script:

```powershell
(Measure-Command {
    $null =Invoke-WebRequest https://postman-echo.com/get?i=1 -SessionVariable Session
    1..10 | ForEach-Object {
            $null =Invoke-WebRequest https://postman-echo.com/get?i=$_ -WebSession $Session
    }
}).ToString()
```

### PowerShell 7.3.3
> 00:00:08.3019013

### PR Branch
> 00:00:03.4589770

issue_context.title: PS 6/7 are 4-5x slower than PS 5 due to not using web connection pool
issue_context.body:
I'm calling an API repeatedly (500,000 times) and I noticed it runs 4-5x faster on PowerShell 5. The code below is not the actual API, but a minimal example that demos the issue.

# Steps to reproduce

I'm running this on 2 different "machines":
- PowerShell 5 and 6 on Windows 10 (physical)
- PowerShell 5 and 7 on Windows Server (VM)

The results are pretty consistent. I noticed PowerShell 6 or 7 for Mac was really slow -- that's why I started benchmarking.

You can adjust `$max` on your machine to get a more reasonable run duration for comparison.

PowerShell Version|Duration (sec.)
:-:|:-:
5|1
6|4
7|5

```powershell
<#
Ver.   Sec
----   ---
   5     1
   6     4
   7     5
#>

$max = 10
$start = Get-Date -Format "HH:mm:ss"
foreach ($i in 1..$max) {
    Invoke-RestMethod "https://postman-echo.com/get?i=$i"
}
$end = Get-Date -Format "HH:mm:ss"
write-host "started at" $start
write-host "  ended at" $end
```
comments: Unless somebody is aware of why this might be, I'm willing to take a look.

PowerShell 6/7 seems to use the HttpClient class which takes about 5-7 seconds of my system under PowerShell 7.0.1 or Windows PowerShell 5:

```
Measure-Command -Expression `
{
   Add-Type -Assembly System.Net.Http
   $Max = 100
   $Size = 0
   ForEach ($I in 1..$Max) 
   {
      $Url = "http://postman-echo.com/get?i=$i"
      $Client = [System.Net.Http.Httpclient]::new()
      $Request = [System.Net.Http.HttpRequestMessage]::new('Get',$Url)
      $CancelToken = [System.Threading.CancellationToken]::new($false)
      $Option = [System.Net.Http.HttpCompletionOption]::ResponseContentRead
      $Response = $Client.SendAsync($Request, $Option, $CancelToken).GetAwaiter().GetResult();
      $Size += $Response.Content.ReadAsByteArrayAsync().Result.Length
   }
   Write-Host 'Total Size' $Size
}
```

Windows PowerShell uses System.Net.WebRequest; this request completes in about 2-3 seconds on my system under Windows PowerShell:

```
Measure-Command -Expression `
{
    $Max = 100
    $Size = 0
    ForEach ($I in 1..$Max) {
        $Url = "http://postman-echo.com/get?i=$i"
        $Request = [System.Net.WebRequest]::Create($Url)
        $Response = $request.BeginGetResponse($null, $null)
        $Response.AsyncWaitHandle.WaitOne()
        $Result= $Request.EndGetResponse($Response)
        $Reader = [System.IO.BinaryReader]::new($Result.GetResponseStream());
        $Size += $Reader.ReadBytes($Result.ContentLength).Length
    }
   Write-Host 'Total Size' $Size
}
```
Interestingly, this latter code also runs much 2x-3x slower under PowerShell 6/7 compared to Windows PowerShell.  This kind of surprised me.

So the question may actually be three-fold: 1) Why the switch to HttpClient? This is not an obvious problem at first glance... just a curiosity.  2) Why is performance so much different between HttpClient and WebRequest under Windows PowerShell, and 3) Why the slowdown in WebRequest from Windows PowerShell to PowerShell Core (may be an underlying DotNet Core question).

WebClient was simply nonexistent in .NET Core during pretty much all of the development of 6.x, and we needed web cmdlets to work with. Even now, it's only really been brought back in for compatibility and isn't recommended for new code as I understand it.

Nor sure about much beyond that, though. 🙂

PowerShell 5 is using a single persistent TCP connection, PowerShell 7 is opening a new connection for each HTTP request.

If the `-DisableKeepAlive` parameter is used with `Invoke-RestMethod` there is no difference in performance.
@NoMoreFood If you set `$Request.KeepAlive = $false` in your example the performance is also the same.
PowerShell 7 actually sends the `Connection: Keep-Alive` header, but than opens a new connection for every request.

According to https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/31267, .NET Core does not currently support TCP KeepAlive in System.Net.HttpClient.

There is an open issue to fix this: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/28721 and underlying issue https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/1793, which are tracking the [5.0 milestone](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/milestone/7). Since PowerShell 7.1 will be targeting .NET 5.0, I expect this issue will be be resolved by the end of 2020.

The problem here is that the `HttpClient` needs to be reused between calls of `Invoke-RestMethod`. This enables connection pooling.

Note that this is _not_ TCP Keepalive (a technology to detect broken idle connections), and the two issues linked above will not help to resolve this.

So the the difference in perfomance is due the fact Windows PowerShell 5 pools connections between seperate instances of `[System.Net.WebRequest]`, and PowerShell 7 does not.

As far as I can see, the only way to ensure use of a persistent connection (in PowerShell 7) is to use a raw `HttpClient` instead of the cmdlets `Invoke-RestMethod`/`Invoke-WebRequest`. Perhaps we could open a new issue to discuss whether to implement this functionality.

I guess I was only partially correct [above](#issuecomment-636546943). Python `requests` has a `Session()` object which allows for [connection pooling](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/master/user/advanced/#session-objects). This only takes about 1 second as opposed to about 4 seconds for the example in my earlier comment (which doesn't use connection pooling).

```python
# Python 3 (with connection pooling)

import requests
from datetime import datetime

session = requests.Session()

MAX = 10
start = datetime.now()
for i in range(MAX):
    session.get(f'https://postman-echo.com/get?i={i}').json()
end = datetime.now()
print('started at', start)
print('  ended at', end)
print(end - start)
```

HttpClient creates SocketsHttpHandler where connection pool is implemented.

If we will share the HttpClient or SocketsHttpHandler per process how do we resolve config conflicts between runspaces?
It seems we can not utilize a global pool.

~~Perhaps we could add new parameter in web cmdlets to get shared SocketsHttpHandler.~~
We could enhance `WebRequestSession` with `SocketsHttpHandler`.
We could utilize a thread-static member to work with that. That'll resolve a majority of cases, and we can have backup code to generate a new handler/client when needed on a secondary thread.
I have a concern about any implicit cache because it can have side effects. We have pool for runspaces. Also we should take into account `ForEach -Parallel`.
for fun, i tried the `-SessionVariable` / `-WebSession` options to see if it would help (kinda like Python above). it didn't.

> 
> 
> for fun, i tried the `-SessionVariable` / `-WebSession` options to see if it would help (kinda like Python above). it didn't.

These parameters did not work for me either to enable connection pooling.
We could enhance `WebRequestSession` with `SocketsHttpHandler`.

> We could utilize a thread-static member to work with that. That'll resolve a majority of cases, and we can have backup code to generate a new handler/client when needed on a secondary thread.

Sorry I am not super familiar with PowerShell, so I am probably misunderstanding. `HttpClient` is thread-safe and does not need a per-thread handler/client -- generally one instance per process works just fine. The only reason to have more than one is if you're setting options on the `SocketsHttpHandler` itself.

There's a lot of caveats here, it looks like. If we could get an agreed on set of requirements for this improvement before work starts, that would be helpful to whoever wants to give it a stab.

I also ran into a problem due to the change in behavior. I have a script that talks to the web server on a Siemens LOGO!8 PLC, it has a very peculiar authentication protocol and I recently discovered the HTTP requests during the handshake need to be sent over the same TCP connection or it doesn't work (obviously this isn't PowerShell's problem but just adding for context). Overall execution of the script in PS 7 was so much snappier than PS 5 that it didn't even occur to me there was a new TCP connection opened each time, although no SSL in my use case. That said, _there is_ at least a documentation issue here: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.utility/invoke-restmethod?view=powershell-7.1 >**-DisableKeepAlive** >Indicates that the cmdlet sets the KeepAlive value in the HTTP header to False. By default, KeepAlive is True. KeepAlive establishes a persistent connection to the server to facilitate subsequent requests. Wireshark shows no `Connection: Keep-Alive` header being sent by default (whereas PowerShell 5.1 does). And `Connection` cannot be specified via the `-Headers` parameter as a workaround either. As previously suggested by @iSazonov I think caching `SocketsHttpHandler` per PS session / runspace would make sense, probably need a separate instance for each set of redirect settings as those get baked as part of the internal message handler chain. However it looks like `SocketsHttpHandler` does the heavy lifting internally as far as adapting to different proxy and retry handling settings. I don't know whether PS presents any special considerations as far as parallelism but believe the best practice with respect to `System.Net.Http.HttpClient` has always been to reuse the instances, or rather reuse the handler, even in highly parallel applications like ASP.NET. Although I'm not sure about _requiring_ the use of `WebRequestSession` to take advantage of connection pooling is a good idea though, the two concerns seem orthogonal. For example you may want to take advantage of connection pooling without sharing cookies (or visa versa).

> @CarloToso Have you interest to work on the issue? I think `WebRequestSession` is designed for this. So we could add new internal field to save SocketsHttpHandler.

I have made an attempt at implementing this; however it's not as straight-forward as just storing a `SocketsHttpHandler` in the WebRequestSession because

1. Current implementation uses `HttpClientHandler`, and the interfaces are different so a lot of parameters that directly set values on the `HttpClientHandler` would need to be updated to translate to similar behaviour on `SocketsHttpHandler`. I have chosen to keep the change minimal and do what you suggested except keeping `HttpClientHandler` instead of changing to `SocketsHttpHandler`.
2. The `HttpClient` is created in a number of places, and uses `using` to ensure it's disposed as soon as it's no longer required. This also causes the associated `HttpClientHandler` to be disposed, so subsequent requests using the same handler will fail because it is already disposed.
3. The `HttpClientHandler` properties are set from the command parameters. Once a handler has been used, these values cannot be changed because they will throw. The only way around this is to do one of the following:
  * compare the new parameters with the old ones and create a new handler if any have changed;
  * ignore any parameters related to setting options on the handler if a websession is passed to the cmdlet; or
  * throw an error if any such parameters are provided and the websession is provided.
 
For problem 2 I have checked for existence of WebSession or SessionVariable parameters and constructed the `HttpClient` with the option to not dispose the handler if either are present. This is not perfect because there is no way to Dispose the handler on sessions that are no longer required without adding additional APIs or switches (e.g. -DisposeSession)

For problem 3 my current implementation uses the second option, simply because it works and was relatively easy to implement.

I compared the performance with/without the change by running on 7.3.1 and the latest main with my changes, routed via Fiddler proxy to validate that no SSL tunnels were being created with the patch (and were without). Note that when using HTTP requests the difference with the patch was only minor.

```powershell
Measure-Command {
    Write-Host (Invoke-WebRequest https://postman-echo.com/get?i=1 -SessionVariable Session).StatusCode
    1..10 | ForEach-Object {
        Invoke-WebRequest https://postman-echo.com/get?i=$_ -WebSession $Session
    }
}
```

I hadn't understood this well enough earlier. All the properties of the WebSession can get updated everytime PrepareSession() method is called so it's definitely possible to have different certificates, proxies, credentials etc on every request. Whether anyone would actually want to do this is anybody's guess, but my limited testing shows that it is possible to do so (e.g. when I supply Proxy to IWR with a session it tries to use the new proxy I supply on each line.

The headers are cumulatively added to the WebSession too, so each time you provide headers argument they override or add to the headers from the last request on the same session (and user agent can be changed just fine on the same session too).

If the workgroup decides that using sessions means you don't get to mess with all those settings between requests then would also need to decide if providing them is considered an error (like providing SessionVar and WebSession together is an error now) and should throw, or should just silently ignore them. At least if it breaks loudly, anyone doing this would know they need to update their scripts rather than it silently ignoring their parameters and not doing what they expected.

The parameters that impact on the use of a persistent handler are anything that gets set into the WebSession that is later set onto the handler in `GetHttpClient`:
* Users could potentially change the `CookieContainer` in the `WebRequestSession` public API
* `UseDefaultCredentials` or `Credentials` changes in the `WebRequestSession` public API, or by providing different parameters for the same items in the `IWR` command line
* `Proxy` is public set in `WebRequestSession` and also via `-Proxy` parameter or `-NoProxy` switch
* `Certificates` is public set in `WebRequestSession` but should be okay when set via `IWR` parameters since it just adds them to the existing container, but only if the container already existed on the first request that initiates the session since the container is created lazily.
* `-SkipCertificateCheck` switch alters the handler's callback if provided on any request - if this were done on the first request it would therefore disable all certificate handling for the session and conversely you wouldn't be able to disable certificate checking for just one request in a sequence of requests in a session.
* `ContentHeaders` and `UserAgent` in `WebRequestSession` should be fine since they are only set on individual requests and not on the handler itself.
* `-MaximumRedirection`, `PreserveAuthorizationOnRedirect` and  `-AllowInsecureRedirect` all have an influence on handler settings for each request.

It looks like `IWR` uses redirection handling in the `HttpClientHandler` except in some specific circumstances where the user specifies authorization and allows insecure redirects because the .net handler explicitly won't do an insecure redirect while authenticating. You can't change this property on the handler after it is constructed so to keep existing behaviour `IWR` might need to always turn off  `HttpClientHandler` redirects and always handle the redirect logic itself. 

An alternative might be to require users to opt-in to more strict session handling through a switch (not sure what would be a good name for it that makes it clear why it's there and what impact it has on the session e.g. `-PersistentSessionVariable MySession`.  The `WebRequestSession` could throw if you try to alter any of the public properties when created using this option.

One concern would be how to use these sessions and get the benefits of a persistent connection while still allowing the user to use a different session but share cookies between sessions in the case they need to alter handling for a single request. The most likely reason I'd want to do this is to disable certificate checks or use test certificates in a test environment for a specific site that may not be setup correctly but keep certificate handling normally for other requests. A workaround would be to allow a new `-PersistentSessionVariable` session to be initialized with an existing cookie container (e.g. from another session ) either using a `-CookieContainer` parameter or by copying from an existing session if both are provided `-PersistentSessionVariable NewSession -WebSession $ExistingSession`. The problem with the latter option is it currently throws when `-SessionVariable NewSession -WebSession $ExistingSession` is passed.

WebRequestSession does not do the check internally because it is using shared code to check for object equality when setting the cookies, proxy, certificates etc. These are publically settable properties on WebSession so can be changed directly in script. In general, these must be updated if the object references aren't the same as the user can modify the properties of the referenced objects after they are set on the WebSession. The WebProxy class is internal so can't easily be constructed by the user, and is a type used directly only by the WebRequestPSCmdlet so it makes sense to add the special case optimisation for not updating the internal proxy class if the cmdlet proxy parameters are identical from invocation to invocation in the class that directly knows about the equality optimisation.

The alternative if to use .Equals() for all reference types in the SetClassVar() function in WebRequestSession, which would be problematic if the equality operator says different references are Equal, but the user tries to modify an object after setting it in the WebRequestSession and it is ignored because of the Equality check.
